items.title: I can explain how accelerating charges produce electromagnetic waves
items.what: Accelerating charges produce oscillating electric fields, which in turn generate oscillating magnetic fields. Together these propagate outward as a transverse electromagnetic wave.
items.why: This is the fundamental mechanism behind all electromagnetic radiation, from radio waves to gamma rays, and explains how antennas and light sources work.
items.example: An electron oscillating in a radio antenna at 100 MHz accelerates back and forth, producing a radio wave of frequency 100 MHz that radiates outward at c.

subtopic.name: Electromagnetic Waves
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the nature of electromagnetic waves as transverse waves produced by accelerating charges. It describes the relationship between oscillating electric and magnetic fields and how all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
subtopic.why: Understanding the wave nature of light underpins all of modern optics, communications technology, and the quantum revolution. It also sets the foundation for understanding why the wave model eventually proved incomplete.

items.title: I can describe the structure of an electromagnetic wave in terms of perpendicular electric and magnetic fields
items.what: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric field (E) and magnetic field (B) oscillate perpendicular to each other and both perpendicular to the direction of travel, forming a transverse wave.
items.why: This structure explains properties like polarisation and confirms that light does not need a medium to travel, unlike sound or water waves.
items.example: A vertically polarised light wave has its E field oscillating vertically, its B field oscillating horizontally, and the wave travelling along a horizontal axis — all three directions are mutually perpendicular.

subtopic.name: Electromagnetic Waves
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the nature of electromagnetic waves as transverse waves produced by accelerating charges. It describes the relationship between oscillating electric and magnetic fields and how all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
subtopic.why: Understanding the wave nature of light underpins all of modern optics, communications technology, and the quantum revolution. It also sets the foundation for understanding why the wave model eventually proved incomplete.

items.title: I can state that all electromagnetic waves travel at speed c in a vacuum and apply the wave equation c = fλ
items.what: All electromagnetic waves, regardless of frequency, travel at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in a vacuum. The wave equation c = fλ relates speed, frequency, and wavelength.
items.why: The universality of c is a cornerstone of physics and essential for calculating properties of any part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
items.example: Green light with wavelength 550 nm has frequency f = c/λ = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 550 × 10⁻⁹ = 5.45 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

subtopic.name: Electromagnetic Waves
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the nature of electromagnetic waves as transverse waves produced by accelerating charges. It describes the relationship between oscillating electric and magnetic fields and how all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
subtopic.why: Understanding the wave nature of light underpins all of modern optics, communications technology, and the quantum revolution. It also sets the foundation for understanding why the wave model eventually proved incomplete.

items.title: I can use the refractive index equation v = c/n to find the speed of light in a medium
items.what: When light enters a medium with refractive index n, it slows to v = c/n. The refractive index is always greater than or equal to 1.
items.why: This explains refraction and dispersion, and is fundamental to the design of lenses, optical fibres, and other optical instruments.
items.example: Glass with n = 1.5 slows light to v = 3.0 × 10⁸ / 1.5 = 2.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the nature of electromagnetic waves as transverse waves produced by accelerating charges. It describes the relationship between oscillating electric and magnetic fields and how all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
subtopic.why: Understanding the wave nature of light underpins all of modern optics, communications technology, and the quantum revolution. It also sets the foundation for understanding why the wave model eventually proved incomplete.

items.title: I can explain how superposition of a wave and its reflection produces a standing wave
items.what: When a travelling wave reflects from a fixed boundary and overlaps with the incoming wave, the principle of superposition causes some points to always cancel (nodes) and others to always reinforce (antinodes).
items.why: Superposition is the same principle that explains interference in Young's double slit experiment, making standing waves a useful conceptual bridge.
items.example: A guitar string fixed at both ends: the player plucks the string, the wave reflects from the nut and bridge, and the superposition of the two waves forms a stable standing wave pattern.

subtopic.name: Standing Waves
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how standing waves form through the superposition of a travelling wave and its reflection. It includes the identification of nodes and antinodes, and analysis of harmonic series in stretched strings.
subtopic.why: Standing waves appear in musical instruments, laser cavities, and microwave ovens. Understanding them requires applying superposition, which is also central to interference phenomena in Young's experiment.

items.title: I can identify nodes and antinodes in a standing wave and describe their properties
items.what: Nodes are points of minimal (zero) oscillation where destructive interference is permanent. Antinodes are points of maximum oscillation, midway between nodes, where constructive interference is permanent.
items.why: Identifying nodes and antinodes allows analysis of standing wave patterns in strings, pipes, and laser cavities.
items.example: In a standing wave on a 60 cm string vibrating in its second harmonic, there are nodes at 0 cm, 30 cm, and 60 cm, with antinodes at 15 cm and 45 cm.

subtopic.name: Standing Waves
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how standing waves form through the superposition of a travelling wave and its reflection. It includes the identification of nodes and antinodes, and analysis of harmonic series in stretched strings.
subtopic.why: Standing waves appear in musical instruments, laser cavities, and microwave ovens. Understanding them requires applying superposition, which is also central to interference phenomena in Young's experiment.

items.title: I can determine the wavelength of a standing wave from the length of the medium and the harmonic number
items.what: For a string with nodes at both ends, the length l must equal a whole number of half-wavelengths: l = nλ/2, so λ = 2l/n for the nth harmonic.
items.why: This relationship allows calculation of wavelength and frequency for any harmonic of a standing wave, which is essential for analysing stringed and wind instruments.
items.example: A 0.30 m string vibrating in its third harmonic: λ = 2 × 0.30 / 3 = 0.20 m.

subtopic.name: Standing Waves
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how standing waves form through the superposition of a travelling wave and its reflection. It includes the identification of nodes and antinodes, and analysis of harmonic series in stretched strings.
subtopic.why: Standing waves appear in musical instruments, laser cavities, and microwave ovens. Understanding them requires applying superposition, which is also central to interference phenomena in Young's experiment.

items.title: I can calculate the frequency of harmonics using fₙ = nv / 2l
items.what: The frequency of the nth harmonic of a standing wave in a string of length l with wave speed v is given by fₙ = nv / 2l. Each harmonic is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency f₁.
items.why: This formula links the physical properties of the medium (length, wave speed) to the frequencies that can form stable standing waves.
items.example: A 0.30 m violin string with wave speed 270 m s⁻¹: f₁ = 1 × 270 / (2 × 0.30) = 450 Hz; f₂ = 900 Hz; f₃ = 1350 Hz.

subtopic.name: Standing Waves
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how standing waves form through the superposition of a travelling wave and its reflection. It includes the identification of nodes and antinodes, and analysis of harmonic series in stretched strings.
subtopic.why: Standing waves appear in musical instruments, laser cavities, and microwave ovens. Understanding them requires applying superposition, which is also central to interference phenomena in Young's experiment.

items.title: I can distinguish between transverse and longitudinal standing waves and give an example of each
items.what: Transverse standing waves have oscillations perpendicular to the direction of travel (e.g. a string). Longitudinal standing waves have oscillations parallel to the direction of travel (e.g. sound in a pipe open at both ends).
items.why: The same superposition principles apply to both types, broadening the range of contexts in which standing wave analysis is applicable.
items.example: A flute open at both ends supports longitudinal standing sound waves, with pressure nodes at each open end — analogous to the displacement nodes at the fixed ends of a string.

subtopic.name: Standing Waves
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how standing waves form through the superposition of a travelling wave and its reflection. It includes the identification of nodes and antinodes, and analysis of harmonic series in stretched strings.
subtopic.why: Standing waves appear in musical instruments, laser cavities, and microwave ovens. Understanding them requires applying superposition, which is also central to interference phenomena in Young's experiment.

items.title: I can describe diffraction as the spreading of a wave through a gap or around an obstacle
items.what: Diffraction is the directional spreading of a wave when it passes through an opening or around an obstacle. It occurs for all wave types including light, sound, and water waves.
items.why: The observation of light diffracting around objects was historically important evidence that light behaves as a wave, since Newton's particle model could not account for it.
items.example: A laser beam passing through a slit of width 0.1 mm spreads into a wider pattern on a screen placed 2 m away, rather than projecting a sharp-edged rectangle of the same width as the slit.

subtopic.name: Diffraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the spreading of waves when they pass through a narrow opening or around an obstacle. It examines the λ/w ratio as a predictor of diffraction spread and its implications for the resolution limits of imaging systems.
subtopic.why: Diffraction sets fundamental limits on the resolution of telescopes, microscopes, and cameras. It also provided early evidence for the wave nature of light and helps explain why the Hubble Space Telescope outperforms the naked eye.

items.title: I can explain qualitatively how the λ/w ratio determines the degree of diffraction
items.what: When λ << w, diffraction is negligible and the wave passes through with little spreading. When λ ≥ w, the slit acts as a point source and the wave spreads through approximately 180°. Intermediate ratios give intermediate spreading.
items.why: This ratio explains why sound (long wavelength) diffracts easily around corners while visible light (short wavelength) does not, and why larger apertures produce sharper images.
items.example: A microwave with λ = 3 cm passing through a gap of w = 2 cm has λ/w > 1 and spreads widely. Visible light (λ ≈ 500 nm) through the same gap has λ/w ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ and spreads very little.

subtopic.name: Diffraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the spreading of waves when they pass through a narrow opening or around an obstacle. It examines the λ/w ratio as a predictor of diffraction spread and its implications for the resolution limits of imaging systems.
subtopic.why: Diffraction sets fundamental limits on the resolution of telescopes, microscopes, and cameras. It also provided early evidence for the wave nature of light and helps explain why the Hubble Space Telescope outperforms the naked eye.

items.title: I can apply the λ/w ratio to explain resolution limits in imaging systems
items.what: Diffraction through the aperture of an eye, camera, or telescope causes images of point sources to spread and overlap. A larger aperture (smaller λ/w) reduces this spreading and improves resolution.
items.why: This is the reason large telescopes can separate closely-spaced stars that appear as a single point to the naked eye, and why UV imaging gives better resolution than visible light imaging.
items.example: Alpha Crucis is a double star. The human eye has a pupil of about 5 mm; a small telescope with an aperture of 80 mm has a 16× larger aperture, producing 16× less diffraction spread and resolving the two stars separately.

subtopic.name: Diffraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the spreading of waves when they pass through a narrow opening or around an obstacle. It examines the λ/w ratio as a predictor of diffraction spread and its implications for the resolution limits of imaging systems.
subtopic.why: Diffraction sets fundamental limits on the resolution of telescopes, microscopes, and cameras. It also provided early evidence for the wave nature of light and helps explain why the Hubble Space Telescope outperforms the naked eye.

items.title: I can use Huygens' wavelet model to explain diffraction qualitatively
items.what: Huygens proposed that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. The envelope of these wavelets forms the new wavefront. At a gap, the wavelets near the edges have no neighbouring wavelets to cancel their sideways spread, so the wave bends around the edges.
items.why: Huygens' model provides a physical mechanism for diffraction without requiring advanced mathematics, and is a useful conceptual tool for visualising wave propagation.
items.example: When a plane wave reaches a narrow slit, only the wavelets originating within the slit continue. Near each edge, these wavelets spread laterally, causing the overall wavefront to fan outward beyond the slit.

subtopic.name: Diffraction
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the spreading of waves when they pass through a narrow opening or around an obstacle. It examines the λ/w ratio as a predictor of diffraction spread and its implications for the resolution limits of imaging systems.
subtopic.why: Diffraction sets fundamental limits on the resolution of telescopes, microscopes, and cameras. It also provided early evidence for the wave nature of light and helps explain why the Hubble Space Telescope outperforms the naked eye.

items.title: I can explain why Young's double slit experiment provides evidence for the wave-like nature of light
items.what: The alternating bright and dark fringes observed in Young's experiment can only be explained by wave superposition — constructive interference producing bright bands and destructive interference producing dark bands. Newton's particle model could not account for the dark bands.
items.why: This experiment was the turning point in the 19th-century debate about the nature of light, and the same wave behaviour had already been established for sound and water waves.
items.example: Two loudspeakers emitting the same frequency produce loud and quiet regions along a line — exactly the same pattern as the bright and dark fringes in Young's light experiment, confirming both are wave phenomena.

subtopic.name: Young's Double Slit Experiment
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the setup, observations, and analysis of Young's double slit experiment. It includes the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of path differences, and the formula for fringe spacing.
subtopic.why: Young's experiment was historically decisive in establishing the wave nature of light. It also introduces coherence as a requirement for observable interference and provides a practical method for measuring the wavelength of light.

items.title: I can state the path difference conditions for constructive and destructive interference
items.what: Bright (constructive) fringes form where the path difference = nλ, where n = 0, 1, 2, ... Dark (destructive) fringes form where the path difference = (n + ½)λ, where n = 0, 1, 2, ...
items.why: These conditions follow directly from the principle of superposition: waves arriving in phase reinforce; waves arriving half a wavelength out of phase cancel.
items.example: At the third bright fringe from the centre, the path difference = 3λ. If λ = 600 nm, the path difference is 1800 nm = 1.8 × 10⁻⁶ m. At the second dark fringe, the path difference = 1.5λ = 900 nm.

subtopic.name: Young's Double Slit Experiment
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the setup, observations, and analysis of Young's double slit experiment. It includes the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of path differences, and the formula for fringe spacing.
subtopic.why: Young's experiment was historically decisive in establishing the wave nature of light. It also introduces coherence as a requirement for observable interference and provides a practical method for measuring the wavelength of light.

items.title: I can calculate fringe spacing using Δx = λL/d and rearrange to find λ, L, or d
items.what: The spacing between adjacent bright (or dark) fringes is Δx = λL/d, where λ is wavelength, L is the slit-to-screen distance, and d is the slit separation. This formula applies when L >> d.
items.why: This formula is used both to measure the wavelength of light in the laboratory and to predict how changing experimental parameters will affect the interference pattern.

subtopic.name: Young's Double Slit Experiment
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the setup, observations, and analysis of Young's double slit experiment. It includes the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of path differences, and the formula for fringe spacing.
subtopic.why: Young's experiment was historically decisive in establishing the wave nature of light. It also introduces coherence as a requirement for observable interference and provides a practical method for measuring the wavelength of light.

items.title: I can predict the effect on fringe spacing of changing λ, L, or d
items.what: From Δx = λL/d: increasing λ or L increases fringe spacing; increasing d decreases fringe spacing. These are direct and inverse proportionalities respectively.
items.why: Predicting these effects tests conceptual understanding of the formula and is commonly assessed in VCE exam questions.
items.example: Replacing a green laser (λ ≈ 530 nm) with a red laser (λ ≈ 650 nm) while keeping L and d constant increases fringe spacing by a factor of 650/530 ≈ 1.23, so 2.0 mm fringes become about 2.5 mm apart.

subtopic.name: Young's Double Slit Experiment
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the setup, observations, and analysis of Young's double slit experiment. It includes the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of path differences, and the formula for fringe spacing.
subtopic.why: Young's experiment was historically decisive in establishing the wave nature of light. It also introduces coherence as a requirement for observable interference and provides a practical method for measuring the wavelength of light.

items.title: I can explain why coherent light sources are required for a clear interference pattern
items.what: Coherent sources are monochromatic and maintain a fixed (or zero) phase difference. Incoherent sources emit light with random phase relationships, washing out the interference pattern.
items.why: This is why lasers produce clearer fringe patterns than filtered white light, and why two separate torches pointed at the same screen will not produce fringes.
items.example: Two separate LEDs aimed at a double slit produce no interference pattern because their phase relationship fluctuates randomly. A single laser split by a double slit produces clear fringes because both slits draw from the same coherent source.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the setup, observations, and analysis of Young's double slit experiment. It includes the conditions for constructive and destructive interference in terms of path differences, and the formula for fringe spacing.
subtopic.why: Young's experiment was historically decisive in establishing the wave nature of light. It also introduces coherence as a requirement for observable interference and provides a practical method for measuring the wavelength of light.

items.title: I can calculate the energy of a photon using E = hf and E = hc/λ
items.what: The energy of a single photon is E = hf = hc/λ, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is Planck's constant. Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) photons carry more energy.
items.why: This formula is the entry point to all quantum optics calculations and is used directly in photoelectric effect problems.
items.example: A photon of green light with λ = 550 nm has energy E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸) / (550 × 10⁻⁹) = 3.62 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.26 eV.

subtopic.name: Photons and Energy
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Einstein's quantisation of light energy, the photon model, and calculations using E = hf = hc/λ in both joules and electronvolts.
subtopic.why: The concept that light energy is quantised into discrete packets (photons) was a radical departure from classical wave theory and is the foundation of all quantum optics and modern photonic technology.

items.title: I can convert photon energies between joules and electronvolts
items.what: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. To convert from eV to joules, multiply by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹. To convert from joules to eV, divide by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹.
items.why: Electronvolts are a more practical unit for atomic-scale energies. VCE exam questions may specify either unit, so fluency in converting between them is essential.
items.example: A photon energy of 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J equals 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.0 eV. Conversely, 2.0 eV = 2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

subtopic.name: Photons and Energy
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Einstein's quantisation of light energy, the photon model, and calculations using E = hf = hc/λ in both joules and electronvolts.
subtopic.why: The concept that light energy is quantised into discrete packets (photons) was a radical departure from classical wave theory and is the foundation of all quantum optics and modern photonic technology.

items.title: I can use Planck's constant in either its J s or eV s form depending on the units required
items.what: Planck's constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s when energy is required in joules, and h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s when energy is required in electronvolts. The choice depends on the units of the answer required.
items.why: Using the correct form of h avoids unnecessary unit conversions and reduces arithmetic errors in multi-step calculations.
items.example: For E in eV: E = hf = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 5.45 × 10¹⁴ = 2.26 eV. For E in joules: E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.45 × 10¹⁴ = 3.61 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Both represent the same photon energy.

subtopic.name: Photons and Energy
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers Einstein's quantisation of light energy, the photon model, and calculations using E = hf = hc/λ in both joules and electronvolts.
subtopic.why: The concept that light energy is quantised into discrete packets (photons) was a radical departure from classical wave theory and is the foundation of all quantum optics and modern photonic technology.

items.title: I can describe the experimental setup and observations of the photoelectric effect
items.what: Light above a threshold frequency strikes a metal surface in an evacuated photocell, ejecting electrons (photoelectrons) that are collected at an electrode, producing a measurable photocurrent. Below the threshold frequency, no electrons are emitted regardless of intensity.
items.why: The specific observations — threshold frequency, independence of kinetic energy from intensity, instantaneous emission — are the phenomena that the wave model failed to explain.
items.example: Zinc requires UV light (high frequency) to emit photoelectrons, while potassium emits photoelectrons under visible light. Increasing the brightness of infrared light on zinc never causes emission — frequency is the controlling factor.

subtopic.name: The Photoelectric Effect
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the experimental observations of the photoelectric effect, Einstein's photon-based explanation, and the limitations of the wave model. It includes analysis of photocurrent vs voltage graphs and Ekmax vs frequency graphs.
subtopic.why: The photoelectric effect provided the first experimental proof of light quantisation, earned Einstein the Nobel Prize, and marked the beginning of quantum physics. It remains a key case study in how experimental evidence can overturn established theory.

items.title: I can interpret a graph of photocurrent versus electrode potential and identify the stopping potential
items.what: As the retarding voltage increases, fewer photoelectrons reach the collector and the current falls. The stopping potential V₀ is the minimum voltage at which the current just reaches zero; it equals Ekmax in eV.
items.why: The stopping potential is the primary experimental measurement for determining the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons, and its independence from intensity is a key piece of evidence against the wave model.
items.example: A photocurrent vs voltage graph shows current falling to zero at −1.2 V. This means the most energetic photoelectrons have Ekmax = 1.2 eV = 1.92 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

subtopic.name: The Photoelectric Effect
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the experimental observations of the photoelectric effect, Einstein's photon-based explanation, and the limitations of the wave model. It includes analysis of photocurrent vs voltage graphs and Ekmax vs frequency graphs.
subtopic.why: The photoelectric effect provided the first experimental proof of light quantisation, earned Einstein the Nobel Prize, and marked the beginning of quantum physics. It remains a key case study in how experimental evidence can overturn established theory.

items.title: I can interpret a graph of Ekmax versus frequency and extract Planck's constant, threshold frequency, and work function
items.what: The graph of Ekmax vs frequency is a straight line with gradient equal to h (Planck's constant), x-intercept equal to the threshold frequency f₀, and y-intercept equal to −φ (the negative of the work function).
items.why: This graph provides a direct experimental method for measuring h and determining the work function of a metal — both fundamental quantities in quantum physics.
items.example: A graph of Ekmax vs f for potassium has a y-intercept of −2.3 eV and crosses the x-axis at 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The work function is φ = 2.3 eV and the threshold frequency is 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

subtopic.name: The Photoelectric Effect
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the experimental observations of the photoelectric effect, Einstein's photon-based explanation, and the limitations of the wave model. It includes analysis of photocurrent vs voltage graphs and Ekmax vs frequency graphs.
subtopic.why: The photoelectric effect provided the first experimental proof of light quantisation, earned Einstein the Nobel Prize, and marked the beginning of quantum physics. It remains a key case study in how experimental evidence can overturn established theory.

items.title: I can apply Ekmax = hf − φ to calculate maximum photoelectron kinetic energy, threshold frequency, or work function
items.what: Einstein's photoelectric equation Ekmax = hf − φ states that the maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron equals the photon energy minus the work function. The work function φ is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal surface.
items.why: This equation is the quantitative core of the photoelectric effect and is used in almost every VCE numerical question on this topic.
items.example: Caesium has φ = 2.10 eV. Green light of frequency 5.45 × 10¹⁴ Hz has photon energy hf = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 5.45 × 10¹⁴ = 2.26 eV. So Ekmax = 2.26 − 2.10 = 0.16 eV = 2.56 × 10⁻²⁰ J.

subtopic.name: The Photoelectric Effect
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the experimental observations of the photoelectric effect, Einstein's photon-based explanation, and the limitations of the wave model. It includes analysis of photocurrent vs voltage graphs and Ekmax vs frequency graphs.
subtopic.why: The photoelectric effect provided the first experimental proof of light quantisation, earned Einstein the Nobel Prize, and marked the beginning of quantum physics. It remains a key case study in how experimental evidence can overturn established theory.

items.title: I can describe the effect of changing light intensity on photocurrent and on Ekmax
items.what: Increasing light intensity at a fixed frequency increases the number of photons per second, which increases the rate of photoelectron emission and therefore increases the photocurrent. However, Ekmax and the stopping potential are unchanged because each individual photon still carries the same energy hf.
items.why: This intensity-independence of Ekmax is one of the most important results that the wave model cannot explain, and it is a standard VCE exam question type.
items.example: Doubling the brightness of a 500 nm light source on a potassium surface doubles the photocurrent (more electrons emitted per second), but the stopping potential remains unchanged at the same value as before.

subtopic.name: The Photoelectric Effect
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the experimental observations of the photoelectric effect, Einstein's photon-based explanation, and the limitations of the wave model. It includes analysis of photocurrent vs voltage graphs and Ekmax vs frequency graphs.
subtopic.why: The photoelectric effect provided the first experimental proof of light quantisation, earned Einstein the Nobel Prize, and marked the beginning of quantum physics. It remains a key case study in how experimental evidence can overturn established theory.

items.title: I can explain why the wave model of light fails to account for key features of the photoelectric effect
items.what: The wave model predicts that any frequency of sufficiently intense light should eventually eject electrons (no threshold frequency), that brighter light should give photoelectrons more kinetic energy (not observed), and that very dim light should cause a measurable delay before emission (not observed).
items.why: Identifying the specific failures of the wave model — and how Einstein's photon model resolves each one — is a key analytical skill required in VCE extended response questions.
items.example: Very faint UV light ejects photoelectrons from zinc almost instantly. The wave model predicts the dim wavefront would need time to deposit enough energy to free an electron. Einstein's model explains this: each UV photon carries enough energy on its own to immediately eject one electron, with no accumulation time needed.
